questions.question: What does RAG stand for and what problem does it solve?
options: Recurrent Attention Generation -- replacing quadratic attention so longer documents fit into the prompt
Reduced Architecture Generation -- shrinking the model so it can be retrained on new documents cheaply
Ranked Answer Grounding -- scoring several candidate answers and returning the one that scores highest
Retrieval-Augmented Generation -- giving LLMs access to external knowledge they weren't trained on
questions.explanation: RAG retrieves relevant documents from an external knowledge base and adds them to the prompt. This gives the LLM access to up-to-date, domain-specific information without retraining.

questions.question: Why is RAG preferred over fine-tuning for most knowledge-grounded applications?
options: RAG bakes your documents permanently into the model's weights, so the answers stay correct even when the vector store is offline or empty
RAG is cheaper, instantly updatable when documents change, and provides source attribution -- fine-tuning is expensive and becomes stale
RAG removes hallucination entirely, since a model handed retrieved passages can only repeat text that already appears in them
RAG teaches the model a style and reasoning pattern that prompting alone cannot reach, which fine-tuning is unable to do
questions.explanation: Fine-tuning costs thousands of dollars, produces a static model that becomes stale as documents change, and offers no source attribution. RAG updates instantly (just update the document store), costs only embedding + storage, and can cite its sources.

questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in a basic RAG pipeline?
options: Embed the documents, generate a draft answer, then chunk that draft and store its embeddings for the next query
Chunk documents, embed chunks, store in vector DB, embed query, retrieve similar chunks, generate answer with context
Embed the query, generate the answer, then retrieve documents afterwards to check the finished answer against them
Store whole documents unchunked, query the LLM first, then append the matching documents to its finished response
questions.explanation: Ingestion: chunk documents -> embed chunks -> store in vector DB. Query time: embed the user's query -> retrieve top-K similar chunks -> add chunks to prompt -> generate answer grounded in retrieved context.

questions.question: What is a common failure mode in basic RAG systems?
options: Retrieved chunks are semantically similar to the query but do not contain the answer, e.g. revenue strategy text when the query asked for Q3 revenue numbers
Cosine similarity cannot compare chunks of different lengths, so long documents always rank ahead of the short chunk holding the answer, however relevant it is
Brute-force cosine search silently drops vectors past the first hundred thousand, so newly added documents are never retrieved at all anymore
Re-indexing after a document changes invalidates every earlier embedding, so the whole vector store has to be rebuilt from scratch each time
questions.explanation: Semantic search finds text that 'sounds like' the query, not necessarily text that 'answers' it. A query about revenue might retrieve chunks discussing revenue strategy rather than the chunk containing the actual number.

questions.question: How do you evaluate RAG quality?
options: By measuring end-to-end latency, since retrieval under 200ms and generation under three seconds define a pipeline that is working correctly
Using both retrieval metrics (did we find the right chunks?) and generation metrics (is the answer faithful to the retrieved context?)
By counting how many chunks were retrieved, since production systems converge on a k of between five and ten chunks per query
By checking that every retrieved chunk falls in the 256 to 512 token range with the standard 50-token overlap between chunks
questions.explanation: RAG evaluation has two parts: retrieval quality (precision/recall of retrieved chunks against ground truth) and generation quality (faithfulness to context, relevance to query, no hallucination beyond retrieved information).
